Title: Garden Tools
Trivia:
A trowel's narrow, curved blade is designed for digging small holes and transplanting seedlings.

Shovels have a curved, scoop-shaped blade, while spades have a flat blade built for cutting straight into soil.

A rake's tines can be rigid for leveling soil or flexible for gathering leaves and debris.

The hoe is one of the oldest gardening tools, used for thousands of years to break up soil and clear weeds.

Hand pruners use a scissor-like action to make clean cuts on stems up to about half an inch thick.

Garden shears are built with longer blades for trimming hedges and shaping shrubs.

A wheelbarrow's single wheel lets one person move heavy loads with far less effort than carrying them.

A spade's flat, sharp edge makes it ideal for edging beds and slicing through turf.

A cultivator's curved prongs are used to loosen and aerate soil before planting.

A dibber is a simple pointed tool used to poke planting holes for seeds and bulbs.

The sickle's curved blade was originally developed for harvesting grain crops by hand.

A mattock combines an axe-like blade with a pick, useful for breaking up hard or rocky ground.

Loppers use long handles to give gardeners the extra leverage needed to cut thick branches.

Secateurs is the British term for what Americans usually call hand pruners.

Title: Popular Flowers
Trivia:
Roses have been cultivated by humans for thousands of years and remain among the most popular cut flowers worldwide.

Tulip bulbs need a period of cold dormancy before they can bloom in spring.

Peonies can live and bloom in the same garden spot for decades without needing to be moved.

Dahlias come in more shapes and sizes than almost any other garden flower, from tiny pompons to dinner-plate blooms.

Zinnias are known for blooming continuously from summer through the first frost.

Carnations get their ruffled petal edges from a trait that also helps give them a long vase life.

Hydrangea flower color can shift between pink and blue depending on the soil's acidity.

Geraniums are prized by gardeners for being both easy to grow and fairly drought tolerant.

Begonias thrive in shady spots where many other flowering plants struggle to bloom.

Pansies can tolerate light frost, making them a favorite for early spring and late fall color.

Chrysanthemums are considered a symbol of autumn and have been cultivated in East Asia for centuries.

Hibiscus flowers usually last only a single day before wilting, despite their large, showy blooms.

Azaleas are technically a type of rhododendron, generally distinguished by smaller leaves and flowers.

Camellias can bloom in the middle of winter, when few other shrubs are flowering.

Title: Vegetable Garden
Trivia:
Tomatoes are botanically a fruit, though they're almost always grown and used as a vegetable.

Peppers range from sweet bell varieties to some of the hottest foods on Earth, all from the same plant genus.

Lettuce grows best in cool weather and can quickly turn bitter once summer heat arrives.

Radishes are one of the fastest vegetables to grow, often ready to harvest in under a month.

Onions are biennial plants, though gardeners almost always harvest them after their first growing season.

Garlic is typically planted in fall and harvested the following summer after nearly a year in the ground.

Potatoes grow underground as swollen stems called tubers, not roots.

Squash plants produce separate male and female flowers on the same vine.

Beets can be grown for both their sweet root and their edible, nutrient-rich leafy greens.

Kale becomes noticeably sweeter after exposure to a light frost.

Celery requires a long, steady growing season and consistent watering to develop its crisp stalks.

Eggplants are members of the nightshade family, related to tomatoes and potatoes.

Okra pods can turn tough and fibrous if left on the plant just a day or two too long.

Chard is prized by gardeners for producing edible leaves all season without needing to be replanted.

Title: Culinary Herbs
Trivia:
Basil is closely related to mint and shares that family's characteristic square-shaped stems.

Thyme is one of the few herbs that keeps much of its flavor even after long cooking or drying.

Rosemary's name comes from a Latin phrase often translated as "dew of the sea," referencing its Mediterranean origins.

Oregano's flavor is generally considered strongest when the plant is dried rather than used fresh.

Cilantro and coriander come from the same plant -- the leaves are called cilantro, the seeds coriander.

Parsley comes in two main forms, curly and flat-leaf, with the flat variety generally having a stronger flavor.

Sage was historically valued not just for cooking but also as a preservative for meats before refrigeration.

Dill is a member of the carrot family, and both its feathery leaves and seeds are used in cooking.

Mint spreads so aggressively by underground runners that gardeners often grow it in containers to contain it.

Chives are among the smallest species in the onion family and regrow quickly after being cut.

Tarragon is a key ingredient in classic French cooking, especially in bearnaise sauce.

Fennel produces both a crunchy, anise-flavored bulb and feathery, edible fronds.

Marjoram is a close relative of oregano but has a milder, sweeter flavor.

Bay leaves are almost always removed from a dish before serving since they stay tough even after cooking.

Title: Fruit Trees
Trivia:
Apple trees grown from seed rarely produce fruit identical to their parent, which is why orchards rely on grafting.

Peach trees need a certain number of cold hours each winter before they'll bloom properly in spring.

Pear trees are sometimes trained flat against a wall or fence using a technique called espalier.

Cherry trees are generally divided into sweet varieties for eating fresh and tart varieties for cooking.

Plum trees come in several types, including European, Japanese, and American, each with different fruit traits.

Apricot trees tend to bloom very early in spring, which can put their flowers at risk from late frosts.

Fig trees can produce fruit without needing pollination at all, depending on the variety.

Lemon trees can flower and fruit at the same time, often nearly year-round in warm climates.

Orange trees are among the most widely planted fruit trees in the world.

Lime trees are generally more cold-sensitive than most other citrus varieties.

Nectarines and peaches are genetically very similar, differing mainly in a gene controlling the fruit's fuzzy skin.

Persimmon trees often keep their bright orange fruit hanging on bare branches well after the leaves have fallen.

Pomegranates are technically classified as a berry, despite their tough outer rind.

Quince fruit is usually too hard and tart to eat raw and is typically cooked into jams or pastes.

Title: Garden Pests
Trivia:
Aphids reproduce so quickly that a single female can give rise to many generations in one growing season.

Slugs are most active at night and after rain, which is when they do the most damage to leafy plants.

Snails carry their protective shell everywhere and can seal themselves inside it during dry spells.

Many beetle species that damage garden plants spend part of their life cycle underground as larvae.

Caterpillars are simply the larval stage of moths and butterflies before they transform.

Weevils are recognizable by their long, curved snout, which they use to bore into plants and seeds.

Mealybugs protect themselves with a white, waxy coating that can make them hard to wash off.

Whiteflies aren't true flies at all -- they're more closely related to aphids.

Cutworms earn their name by chewing through young seedling stems right at the soil line.

Grubs are the larval stage of beetles and often live underground, feeding on plant roots.

Spider mites are so small that gardeners often notice their fine webbing before they spot the mites themselves.

Thrips are tiny, slender insects that can spread plant diseases as they feed.

Tomato hornworms can strip a plant of its leaves remarkably fast for their size.

Leafhoppers can jump many times their own body length to escape predators.

Title: Pollinators and Beneficial Insects
Trivia:
Bees are responsible for pollinating a huge share of the world's flowering food crops.

Butterflies taste with sensors on their feet, helping them identify the right plants to lay eggs on.

Ladybugs can eat dozens of aphids in a single day, making them a gardener's natural ally.

Hoverflies mimic the black-and-yellow coloring of bees and wasps despite being harmless flies.

Bumblebees can fly in cooler temperatures than most other bees, making them important early-season pollinators.

Some wasp species are highly beneficial in gardens because they prey on caterpillars and other pest insects.

Moths pollinate many night-blooming flowers that bees rarely if ever visit.

Dragonflies are effective predators of mosquitoes and other small flying insects.

The praying mantis is a patient ambush predator that will eat almost any insect it can catch.

Lacewing larvae are sometimes called "aphid lions" for how many aphids they consume.

Honeybees communicate the location of food sources to each other through a distinctive waggle dance.

Hummingbirds have such high energy needs that they visit hundreds of flowers a day for nectar.

Many garden spiders are beneficial predators that help keep insect pest populations in check.

Earthworms improve soil structure and fertility as they tunnel through the ground and break down organic matter.

Title: Soil and Composting
Trivia:
Compost forms as microorganisms break down organic material like food scraps and yard waste into rich, dark soil.

A layer of mulch helps soil retain moisture and suppresses weed growth at the same time.

Humus is the dark, stable organic matter left after decomposition is mostly complete, and it improves soil quality.

Loam is considered ideal garden soil because it balances sand, silt, and clay in roughly equal parts.

Clay soil holds water and nutrients well but can become compacted and drain poorly.

Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay, giving silty soil a smooth, floury texture.

Nitrogen is one of the three main nutrients plants need most, supporting healthy leaf and stem growth.

Phosphorus supports strong root development and helps plants flower and produce fruit.

Potassium helps plants regulate water use and supports overall disease resistance.

Microbes in healthy soil break down organic matter and make nutrients available to plant roots.

Fallen leaves and food scraps decompose faster when they're chopped smaller before being added to a compost pile.

Aerating soil relieves compaction, letting air, water, and roots move through it more easily.

Soil acidity is measured on a pH scale, and most garden plants prefer a slightly acidic to neutral range.

Plants absorb nutrients from the soil through their root systems, dissolved in water.

Title: Pruning and Trimming
Trivia:
Pruning at the right time of year helps a plant heal quickly and encourages healthy new growth.

Trimming hedges regularly keeps them dense by encouraging branching along their outer edges.

Deadheading spent flowers often encourages a plant to keep producing new blooms instead of setting seed.

Thinning out crowded branches improves airflow and lets more sunlight reach the remaining growth.

Careful shaping over several seasons can train a young shrub into almost any desired form.

A clean cut heals faster and is less likely to invite disease than a ragged or torn one.

A well-maintained hedge can serve as a living fence, privacy screen, or garden border.

Topiary is the art of pruning trees and shrubs into precise, often geometric or animal-shaped forms.

A bud is the undeveloped growth point on a plant that can become a new leaf, stem, or flower.

A plant's stem provides structural support and transports water and nutrients between roots and leaves.

Removing a damaged or diseased branch promptly can protect the rest of the plant from further harm.

Suckers are vigorous shoots that grow from a plant's base or roots and often need to be removed.

Trees seal off pruning wounds by forming a callus of new tissue around the cut edge.

Scaffold branches form a tree's main structural framework and are chosen carefully when young trees are pruned.

Title: Types of Gardens
Trivia:
Cottage gardens are known for their informal, densely packed mix of flowers, herbs, and vegetables.

Formal gardens rely on symmetry and carefully clipped hedges to create a structured, geometric look.

Rock gardens use stones and gravel to create a well-drained home for alpine and drought-tolerant plants.

Container gardening lets people grow plants in pots, making it possible even without any ground soil.

Raised bed gardens improve drainage and let gardeners control soil quality more precisely than in-ground beds.

Vertical gardens grow plants upward on walls, trellises, or stacked structures to save ground space.

A kitchen garden is grown specifically to supply fresh vegetables and herbs for everyday cooking.

A butterfly garden is planted specifically with nectar and host plants to attract and support butterflies.

Rain gardens are planted in low spots to capture and filter stormwater runoff naturally.

Zen gardens use raked gravel or sand alongside carefully placed rocks to encourage calm reflection.

Tropical gardens rely on bold foliage and lush, layered plantings to create a rainforest-like feel.

Desert gardens favor cacti and succulents specifically chosen to thrive with very little water.

Community gardens give neighbors shared plots of land to grow food and flowers together.

Woodland gardens are planted beneath trees, favoring shade-loving plants like ferns and hostas.

Title: Watering and Irrigation
Trivia:
Sprinkler systems can be programmed to water gardens automatically at efficient times of day.

A quality garden hose is rated by both its diameter and its resistance to kinking.

Drip irrigation delivers water slowly and directly to plant roots, wasting far less than overhead sprinklers.

A nozzle's spray pattern can often be adjusted from a fine mist to a strong, focused jet.

A rain barrel or reservoir lets gardeners store and reuse water collected from rooftops.

Soaker hoses release water gradually along their entire length through thousands of tiny pores.

A timer can automate a watering system so gardens are watered consistently even when no one's home.

Rainwater is naturally free of the chlorine and minerals often found in tap water.

Overwatering is one of the most common mistakes new gardeners make, often causing root problems.

Drought-tolerant plants have adapted to survive extended periods with very little available water.

Checking soil moisture before watering helps prevent both overwatering and underwatering.

A spigot, or outdoor faucet, is usually the starting point for a garden's entire watering setup.

A shutoff valve lets gardeners control water flow to different parts of an irrigation system independently.

A cistern collects and stores large volumes of rainwater, historically a critical water source before modern plumbing.

Title: Garden Structures
Trivia:
A trellis gives climbing plants like vines and beans a structure to grow up instead of sprawling.

An arbor typically frames an entryway or path, often draped with climbing roses or vines.

A pergola provides partial shade with an open, slatted roof structure supported by posts or columns.

Greenhouses trap heat and sunlight, letting gardeners grow plants outside their normal outdoor season.

A gazebo offers a fully roofed, open-sided shelter, often used as a garden's central gathering spot.

Garden fences can serve as decoration, wind protection, or a barrier to keep animals out.

A garden shed provides dedicated storage for tools, pots, and supplies close to where they're used.

A cold frame acts like a mini unheated greenhouse, protecting young plants from frost using sunlight alone.

Planters let gardeners grow plants above ground level, useful on patios or where soil quality is poor.

Stakes support tall or heavy plants like tomatoes so their stems don't bend or break.

An obelisk-shaped support gives climbing plants a tall, narrow structure to twine around.

An archway can mark a transition between different garden rooms or frame a scenic view.

A birdhouse gives cavity-nesting birds a safe place to raise their young in the garden.

A well-planned walkway guides visitors through a garden while protecting planting beds from foot traffic.

Title: Seeds and Propagation
Trivia:
A seed contains a tiny embryonic plant along with a store of food to fuel its first growth.

Germination begins when a seed absorbs water and its embryo starts to grow.

A seedling is a young plant in its earliest stage of growth after germination.

Taking a cutting from an existing plant lets gardeners grow a genetically identical new plant.

Grafting joins tissue from two different plants so they grow together as one.

Dividing an overgrown perennial creates several new plants and helps rejuvenate its growth.

Rootstock is the root system a fruit tree variety is often grafted onto for hardiness or size control.

Dormant seeds can remain viable for years, waiting for the right conditions to germinate.

A sprout is the very first visible growth to emerge once a seed germinates.

Pollination transfers pollen between flowers, allowing plants to produce seeds and fruit.

Hybrid seeds are produced by intentionally cross-pollinating two different plant varieties.

Heirloom seeds come from open-pollinated plant varieties passed down for generations, breeding true from year to year.

Seed viability naturally declines over time, so older seeds germinate less reliably.

Stratifying seeds in cold, moist conditions mimics winter and can trigger some species to germinate.

Title: Lawn Care
Trivia:
A mower with sharp blades cuts grass cleanly instead of tearing it, keeping the lawn healthier.

Turf refers to the layer of grass and the soil held together by its roots.

Thatch is a layer of dead grass and roots that can build up between the soil and living grass.

Aerating a lawn relieves soil compaction, helping water, air, and nutrients reach grass roots.

Overseeding fills in thin or bare patches by spreading new grass seed over an existing lawn.

Fertilizing at the right time of year gives lawns the nutrients they need for dense, green growth.

Sod is pre-grown turf that can be installed for an instant lawn instead of waiting for seed to grow.

Leaving grass clippings on the lawn after mowing can return nutrients back into the soil.

A mower blade should be sharpened regularly to avoid shredding grass tips and stressing the lawn.

Dethatching removes built-up dead plant material so grassroots can access water and nutrients more easily.

Crabgrass is a fast-spreading warm-season weed that thrives in thin, stressed lawns.

Irrigating deeply but less frequently encourages grass roots to grow stronger and deeper.

Dandelions have deep taproots that make them notoriously difficult to fully remove from a lawn.

A healthy lawn helps prevent soil erosion and can cool the surrounding air on hot days.

Title: Houseplants
Trivia:
Pothos is prized as a beginner-friendly houseplant that tolerates low light and irregular watering.

Philodendrons are popular houseplants partly because they can thrive across a range of indoor light levels.

Succulents store water in their thick leaves, letting them tolerate infrequent watering.

Ferns generally prefer high humidity, which is why they're often grown successfully in bathrooms.

Ivy is a fast-growing vining plant often trained to climb or trail from hanging baskets.

Monstera plants develop their signature leaf holes, called fenestrations, as the plant matures.

Orchids are often grown in bark or moss instead of regular potting soil, mimicking their natural growing conditions.

Begonias grown indoors are prized for their colorful, often asymmetrical leaves as much as their flowers.

Peperomia plants are compact and come in a wide range of leaf textures and patterns.

Dracaena plants are popular for their architectural, strappy leaves and tolerance of indoor conditions.

Aloe vera gel from its leaves has long been used to soothe minor burns and skin irritation.

Ficus trees are a common indoor choice but can drop leaves if moved or exposed to drafts.

Cactus plants generally need much less frequent watering indoors than most other houseplants.

Bromeliads often form a central "cup" that collects water in their natural rainforest habitat.

Title: Succulents and Cacti
Trivia:
Saguaro cacti grow extremely slowly and can take decades before growing their first side arm.

Echeveria succulents form neat, symmetrical rosettes that make them popular in succulent arrangements.

Agave plants often live for many years before flowering just once and then dying.

Aloe plants store water in thick, gel-filled leaves adapted for arid conditions.

Jade plants can live for decades and are sometimes passed down as houseplants between generations.

Sedum varieties range from low groundcovers to taller upright types, all valued for drought tolerance.

Barrel cacti tend to lean slightly toward the sun as they grow.

Haworthia plants often have translucent "windows" on their leaf tips to help capture light underground in the wild.

Kalanchoe is popular for its clusters of small, long-lasting flowers atop fleshy leaves.

Yucca plants have stiff, sword-shaped leaves and can survive in poor, dry soil.

Opuntia, or prickly pear, produces edible pads and fruit alongside its sharp spines.

Lithops are nicknamed "living stones" because they closely resemble the pebbles among which they grow.

A cactus's spines are modified leaves that also help reduce water loss.

Many succulents form a tight rosette shape that helps shade their own center and reduce water evaporation.

Title: Roses
Trivia:
Hybrid tea roses are known for producing large, classic single blooms on long stems, popular for cut flowers.

Climbing roses can be trained along fences, trellises, and arbors to grow many feet upward.

Shrub roses tend to be hardier and lower-maintenance than many other rose types.

Floribunda roses produce blooms in clusters rather than one flower per stem.

A rose's thorns are technically called prickles, since they grow from the outer layer of the stem.

Rose petals are edible and are sometimes used in teas, syrups, and desserts.

A rose bloom typically opens gradually over several days from a tightly wrapped bud.

A rosebud is the tightly furled early stage of a flower before its petals open.

Rose hips, the fruit left after petals fall, are rich in vitamin C and used in teas and jams.

Fragrance varies enormously between rose varieties, with some modern types bred more for color than scent.

A rose cane is one of its main woody stems, which is pruned back to encourage new growth.

Roses are commonly propagated by grafting a chosen variety onto hardier rootstock.

Deadheading spent rose blooms often encourages the bush to keep producing new flowers.

There are thousands of named rose varieties, ranging from tiny miniatures to towering climbers.

Title: Trees and Shrubs
Trivia:
Oak trees can live for several hundred years and support an enormous number of wildlife species.

Maple trees are the source of the sap used to make maple syrup.

Birch trees are known for their distinctive white, papery bark that peels in thin layers.

Willow trees are fast-growing and often planted near water, where their roots help control erosion.

Magnolias are among the most ancient flowering plant lineages still alive today.

Juniper shrubs are valued in landscaping for staying green through winter and tolerating poor soil.

Boxwood is a classic choice for clipped, formal hedges because it responds well to frequent trimming.

Holly shrubs are known for their glossy, spiny leaves and bright red winter berries.

Lilac shrubs are prized for their fragrant purple or white blooms in spring.

Forsythia is often one of the very first shrubs to bloom, signaling the start of spring with bright yellow flowers.

Spirea shrubs produce dense clusters of small flowers and are valued for their low-maintenance nature.

Dogwood trees produce distinctive four-petaled flowers in spring, followed by berries favored by birds.

Elm trees were once widely planted as street trees before Dutch elm disease devastated many populations.

Spruce trees have stiff, sharp needles attached individually to the branch, unlike the softer needles of firs.

Title: Garden Design
Trivia:
Symmetry in garden design creates a formal, orderly feeling by mirroring elements on either side of a central line.

A focal point draws the eye and gives a garden a clear visual anchor, like a specimen tree or sculpture.

Garden borders frame planting beds and help define the edges of a space.

A well-planned pathway guides visitors through a garden while protecting the surrounding plants.

A garden's overall layout determines how different areas and features relate to one another.

Mixing leaf textures, from fine and feathery to broad and glossy, adds visual interest even without flowers.

Color theory helps gardeners choose plant combinations that either harmonize or create striking contrast.

Scale considers how the size of plants and structures relates to the overall space and each other.

Balance in garden design doesn't require symmetry -- it can also come from thoughtfully placed asymmetry.

Repeating certain plants or colors throughout a garden helps tie separate areas together visually.

A hedge or wall can serve as a backdrop that makes brighter plants in front stand out.

A framed vista draws the eye toward a distant view, whether natural scenery or a garden feature.

A limited color palette often reads as more sophisticated than planting every color at once.

Choosing a unifying theme, like a Mediterranean or cottage style, helps guide every design decision.

Title: Fertilizing and Feeding
Trivia:
Well-aged animal manure adds organic matter and nutrients to garden soil, but fresh manure can burn plant roots.

Granular fertilizers release their nutrients gradually as they break down in the soil.

Liquid fertilizers are absorbed quickly, making them useful for giving plants a fast nutrient boost.

Organic fertilizers come from plant or animal sources and typically feed soil life as well as plants.

Synthetic fertilizers are manufactured to deliver specific, precisely measured nutrient ratios.

Slow-release fertilizers are coated so their nutrients become available gradually over weeks or months.

Top-dressing spreads a thin layer of compost or fertilizer directly onto the soil surface around existing plants.

Foliar feeding applies liquid nutrients directly to a plant's leaves for rapid absorption.

Bone meal is a slow-release organic fertilizer especially valued for its phosphorus content.

Fish emulsion is a liquid organic fertilizer made from processed fish byproducts.

Garden lime raises soil pH, making acidic soil less sour for plants that prefer neutral conditions.

Gypsum can improve heavy clay soil structure without significantly changing its pH.

A balanced fertilizer supplies roughly equal amounts of the three primary plant nutrients.

Vermicompost is nutrient-rich compost produced with the help of earthworms digesting organic matter.

Title: Gardening Through the Seasons
Trivia:
As soil begins to thaw in early spring, it becomes workable again after being frozen solid all winter.

Many spring bulbs are among the first plants to bloom once the weather starts warming.

Fruit generally ripens fastest during the warm, sunny days of mid-to-late summer.

Harvest time varies enormously by crop, from quick spring radishes to fall's winter squash.

Dormancy lets many plants survive winter's cold by essentially pausing their growth until spring.

Transplanting seedlings outdoors is best timed to avoid the last expected frost of spring.

Acclimating seedlings gradually to outdoor conditions before transplanting helps them avoid stress and shock.

Tender plants that can't survive freezing temperatures must be brought indoors to overwinter.

Succession planting means sowing new crops every few weeks for a continuous harvest all season.

Rotating where crops are planted each year helps prevent soil-borne diseases from building up.

Perennial plants live for multiple years, regrowing from the same roots each season.

Annual plants complete their entire life cycle, from seed to death, within a single year.

Biennial plants take two years to complete their life cycle, usually flowering only in the second year.

A plant's hardiness rating indicates the coldest winter temperatures it can typically survive.

Title: Butterfly and Wildlife Gardens
Trivia:
Milkweed is the only plant monarch butterfly caterpillars are able to eat.

Flowers produce nectar specifically to attract and reward the pollinators that visit them.

A host plant is one a particular insect species needs in order to lay eggs and complete its life cycle.

Inside a chrysalis, a caterpillar undergoes a dramatic transformation into a butterfly.

A larva is an insect's early life stage, dramatically different in form from the adult it will become.

Monarch butterflies undertake one of the longest known insect migrations, traveling thousands of miles each year.

Swallowtail butterflies are named for the pointed, tail-like extensions on their hind wings.

A birdbath gives birds a reliable water source for both drinking and bathing.

A well-stocked bird feeder can attract a wide variety of species to a garden year-round.

Creating habitat with native plants gives local wildlife the food and shelter they've adapted to rely on.

A wildlife sanctuary garden is planted specifically to support and protect local birds, insects, and small animals.

Moths, like butterflies, typically spend time inside a protective cocoon during their transformation.

Bird migration patterns are closely tied to the seasonal availability of food sources like insects and berries.

Pollinator populations worldwide benefit from gardens that avoid pesticides and offer a variety of blooming plants.

Title: Companion Planting
Trivia:
Marigolds are commonly planted alongside vegetables because their scent is thought to help repel certain pests.

Nasturtiums are often used as a "trap crop," luring pests away from more valuable vegetables nearby.

Borage draws in extra pollinators, and a controlled study found strawberries planted near it yielded noticeably more fruit.

Chamomile is sometimes called a "physician plant" for its old reputation of improving the health of nearby crops.

Basil is traditionally planted near tomatoes, a pairing gardeners have used for generations.

Dill can attract beneficial predatory insects that help control pests on nearby vegetables.

Carrots and onions are often paired because each plant's scent may help mask the other from pests.

Beans, along with corn and squash, form the traditional "Three Sisters" planting method used by Indigenous farmers.

Corn provides a natural support structure for climbing bean vines to grow up in companion plantings.

Squash's broad leaves shade the soil, helping to suppress weeds around companion-planted corn and beans.

Interplanting different crops together can make more efficient use of garden space and confuse pest insects.

Some companion plants are chosen specifically to repel insects that would otherwise damage nearby crops.

Other companion plants work by attracting beneficial insects that prey on common garden pests.

The overall synergy between well-chosen companion plants can improve garden health more than growing each crop alone.

Title: Flower Bulbs
Trivia:
Tulip bulbs are planted in fall so they can experience the cold winter needed to trigger spring blooming.

Daffodils contain a natural toxin that keeps squirrels and deer from eating the bulbs.

Crocuses are often among the very first flowers to bloom, sometimes even pushing up through snow.

Hyacinths are prized for their powerful fragrance, produced by densely packed flower spikes.

Bearded iris rhizomes should be planted with their top partly exposed above the soil surface.

True lilies grow from scaly bulbs and are unrelated to daylilies despite the similar name.

Gladiolus spikes can grow several feet tall, with flowers opening gradually from the bottom up.

Amaryllis bulbs are popular for winter forcing, producing enormous blooms indoors during the colder months.

Allium flowers form striking round flower clusters and belong to the same family as onions and garlic.

Anemone flowers come in both fall-planted and spring-planted types, depending on the variety.

Ranunculus plants grow from small claw-shaped corms and produce some of the most densely petaled blooms in the garden.

Freesias are especially valued in bouquets for their sweet fragrance.

Snowdrops are known for blooming extremely early, sometimes while there's still snow on the ground.

Calla lilies grow from rhizomes and produce a single, elegantly curved petal-like bract around each flower spike.

Title: Common Garden Weeds
Trivia:
Thistles produce deep taproots and sharp spines that make them tough to remove by hand.

Clover is sometimes tolerated or even encouraged in lawns since it can add nitrogen back into the soil.

Chickweed spreads quickly in cool weather and can form a dense mat across bare soil.

Plantain weed has broad, ribbed leaves and is unrelated to the banana-like plantain fruit.

Bindweed twines tightly around other plants and can be extremely difficult to fully eliminate once established.

Nutsedge is often mistaken for grass but can be identified by its triangular stem.

Pokeweed produces berries that are toxic to humans, though many birds can eat them safely.

Ragweed pollen is one of the most common triggers of seasonal allergies in late summer and fall.

Nettles can deliver a stinging, itchy reaction when touched, thanks to tiny hollow hairs on their leaves.

Burdock produces round, spiky seed heads that are famously credited with inspiring hook-and-loop fastener.

Henbit is a low-growing winter weed easily identified by its small purple flowers in early spring.

Purslane is edible and surprisingly nutritious, though most gardeners still treat it as an unwanted weed.

Ground ivy spreads along the soil surface by rooting wherever its trailing stems touch the ground.

Spurge plants release a milky sap when broken that can irritate skin on contact.

Title: Native Plants and Wildflowers
Trivia:
Purple coneflower, or echinacea, is a native prairie plant popular with both pollinators and gardeners.

Black-eyed Susans are hardy native wildflowers recognized by their bright yellow petals and dark center.

Asters bloom in late summer and fall, providing crucial late-season nectar for migrating pollinators.

Goldenrod is often mistakenly blamed for hay fever, though its pollen is too heavy and sticky to travel far in the air.

Lupine flowers grow in tall spikes and belong to the same family as peas and beans.

Lobelia comes in both native wildflower species and popular garden varieties prized for vivid blue flowers.

Liatris, also called blazing star, produces tall purple flower spikes that bloom from the top down.

Lavender is beloved for its calming fragrance and its ability to thrive in dry, sunny conditions.

Prairie ecosystems historically supported an enormous diversity of native grasses and flowering plants.

A wildflower meadow can provide season-long food and habitat for a wide range of pollinators.

Indigenous peoples across North America cultivated and used native plants for food, medicine, and craft for millennia.

A garden planted with native species supports the local ecosystem more effectively than many exotic ornamentals.

Butterflies rely heavily on specific native plants for both nectar as adults and food as caterpillars.

Wildflower gardens generally require less water and fertilizer than traditional ornamental flower beds.

Title: Vines and Climbing Plants
Trivia:
Ivy clings to surfaces using small root-like structures that grip onto brick, wood, or bark.

Clematis vines are sometimes called the "queen of climbers" for their large, showy flowers.

Wisteria vines can grow remarkably fast and heavy, requiring sturdy support structures to bear their weight.

Honeysuckle flowers produce a sweet nectar that hummingbirds and butterflies find highly attractive.

Morning glory flowers typically open at dawn and close again by the afternoon heat.

A grapevine's tendrils coil tightly around supports, pulling the growing vine upward as it climbs.

Jasmine vines are grown around the world primarily for their intensely sweet evening fragrance.

Trumpet vine produces large, tubular flowers that are especially attractive to hummingbirds.

Passionflower vines produce intricate, unusually shaped blooms followed by edible fruit in some varieties.

Bougainvillea's colorful display actually comes from papery bracts surrounding its much smaller true flowers.

A tendril is a thin, thread-like structure some climbing plants use to grip onto supports.

Twining vines wind their entire stem around a support, rather than using tendrils or clinging roots.

Climbing plants let gardeners add greenery and flowers vertically, even in small garden spaces.

A lattice provides an open, crisscrossed framework that gives young climbing plants something to grip early on.

Title: Ornamental Grasses
Trivia:
Fountain grass gets its name from its arching, spray-like clumps of narrow foliage.

Pampas grass can grow into towering clumps topped with large, feathery plumes in late summer.

Bamboo is technically a type of grass and includes some of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.

Fescue is a cool-season grass often chosen for lawns in cooler climates.

Sedges resemble grasses but often have distinctly triangular stems, unlike true grasses' round ones.

Miscanthus varieties are popular ornamental grasses valued for their height and graceful, arching form.

Little bluestem is a native prairie grass known for turning a striking reddish-bronze color in fall.

Switchgrass is a hardy native prairie grass also used for erosion control and biofuel production.

Zoysia grass is prized in warm climates for forming a dense, carpet-like lawn.

Bermuda grass spreads aggressively by both underground and above-ground runners, making it hard to contain.

Ryegrass germinates quickly, which is why it's often used to overseed lawns for fast results.

Feather grass produces long, silky seed heads that sway dramatically in even a light breeze.

A grass plume is the feathery flowering seed head that rises above many ornamental grass varieties.

Grass blades grow continuously from their base, which is why mowing doesn't harm the plant.

Title: Water Gardens and Ponds
Trivia:
A backyard pond can support fish, aquatic plants, and a surprising variety of visiting wildlife.

Water lilies root in mud at the pond bottom while their flowers and leaves float on the surface.

Lotus flowers are known for rising well above the water on tall stems, unlike lower-floating water lilies.

Koi fish are a domesticated, ornamental variety of carp bred for their bright colors and patterns.

A cascading water feature adds both movement and soothing sound to a garden pond.

A pond filter helps keep water clear by removing debris and supporting beneficial bacteria.

A flexible pond liner creates a watertight basin, letting gardeners build a pond almost anywhere.

Aquatic plants help oxygenate pond water and provide shelter for fish and other wildlife.

Algae growth in a pond is often controlled by balancing sunlight, nutrients, and plant coverage.

Reeds growing at a pond's edge help filter runoff and provide habitat for wildlife.

A lily pad's waxy, water-repellent surface helps keep it floating clear of standing water.

A biofilter uses beneficial bacteria to break down fish waste and keep pond water healthy.

A pump keeps pond water circulating, which helps prevent stagnation and supports oxygen levels.

A garden waterfall recirculates water from a pond, adding both sound and aeration to the feature.

Title: Bonsai and Topiary
Trivia:
Bonsai is the centuries-old art of growing and shaping miniature trees in containers.

Topiary involves training and clipping living plants into precise decorative or geometric shapes.

Careful, regular pruning keeps a bonsai tree small while encouraging a mature, tree-like form.

Bonsai growers use thin wire to gently bend and train branches into a desired shape as they grow.

Training a plant's growth over months or years is central to both bonsai and topiary traditions.

Despite their tiny size, bonsai trees are the same species as their full-sized counterparts.

A bonsai's trunk is often shaped to suggest great age and character within a small container.

A tree's canopy is carefully thinned and shaped in bonsai to mimic a mature tree's silhouette.

Nebari refers to the visible surface root flare at a bonsai's base, prized for its aged appearance.

Bonsai trees need to be repotted periodically to refresh their soil and trim their confined root systems.

A shallow bonsai tray is chosen specifically to restrict root growth and help keep the tree miniature.

Junipers are among the most popular species for bonsai because they tolerate heavy pruning and shaping well.

Maple trees are prized in bonsai for their delicate leaves and vibrant fall color.

Both bonsai and topiary demand tremendous patience, since dramatic results often take years to achieve.

Title: Sunflowers
Trivia:
Young sunflowers exhibit heliotropism, tracking the sun across the sky before maturing and typically facing east.

Each sunflower "flower" is actually made of hundreds of tiny petals arranged around a central disc.

A single sunflower seedhead can contain over a thousand individual seeds.

A sunflower's thick stalk can grow more than ten feet tall in a single season.

Sunflowers produce abundant pollen that's highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.

The tallest recorded sunflowers have reached heights of over 30 feet.

Most garden sunflowers are annuals, completing their life cycle in a single growing season.

Hybrid sunflower varieties are often bred for pollen-free blooms, making them popular as cut flowers.

Commercial sunflower hybrids are selected for traits like disease resistance and seed yield.

Sunflower seeds are pressed to produce a widely used cooking oil.

The sunflower's golden color comes from pigments that also help attract pollinators.

The central disc of a sunflower is made up of hundreds of small individual florets.

The seeds within a sunflower head are arranged in a natural spiral pattern following a mathematical sequence.

Sunflower seed heads are typically harvested once the back of the head turns brown and dry.

Title: Tulips
Trivia:
Tulip bulbs need a period of cold dormancy before they'll bloom in spring.

A tulip's petals form a distinctive cup or goblet shape when the flower opens.

The Dutch became closely associated with tulips after a 17th-century speculative bulb-trading boom.

Tulips are among the earliest and most recognizable signs of spring in many gardens.

Hybrid tulips are bred for traits like color, fringe patterns, or extended bloom time.

The goblet-shaped bloom helps protect a tulip's reproductive parts from rain and cold.

Thousands of tulip varieties exist, ranging from simple single-color blooms to elaborately fringed types.

A tulip cultivar is a specific variety bred and maintained for consistent characteristics.

Tulip bulbs are generally hardy but can be damaged by a late, hard frost after sprouting.

Tulip blooms typically last only one to two weeks before petals begin to drop.

Tulip stems continue to grow slightly even after the flowers are cut for a vase.

Tulip bulbs are traditionally planted in autumn, several weeks before the ground freezes.

Tulips come in nearly every color except true blue.

Tulip bulbs were originally imported to Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century.

Title: Daffodils
Trivia:
A daffodil's central trumpet-shaped structure is technically called the corona.

Daffodil bulbs multiply underground over time, producing more blooms in following years.

Daffodils belong to the genus Narcissus, named in Greek mythology.

Many daffodil varieties have a slightly nodding, downward-facing bloom.

The corona at a daffodil's center is often a different color than its outer petals.

Daffodils are known for naturalizing, spreading and multiplying on their own once established.

Daffodils are among the earliest bulbs to bloom, often appearing while snow still lingers.

Bright yellow is the most iconic daffodil color, though white and orange varieties also exist.

Daffodils are perennial bulbs, returning reliably year after year with minimal care.

Some daffodil varieties produce multiple blooms in a cluster on a single stem.

A daffodil's stem is hollow, which helps it stay upright despite its relatively large bloom.

Certain daffodil varieties are prized for a strong, sweet fragrance.

Daffodils are organized into official divisions based on flower shape and parentage.

Daffodils are one of the most reliable and widely planted spring-flowering bulbs.

Title: Orchids
Trivia:
Many orchid species are epiphytes, growing on other plants rather than in soil.

Epiphytic orchids use specialized aerial roots to absorb moisture and nutrients from the air.

The orchid family, Orchidaceae, is one of the largest families of flowering plants on Earth.

Orchid pollen is packaged into waxy masses called pollinia rather than loose grains.

The comet orchid famously evolved alongside a specific moth species with an extremely long tongue.

Vanilla, used widely in baking, actually comes from the seed pods of a climbing orchid.

Orchids are typically potted in chunky bark mix rather than traditional soil, since their roots need airflow.

Most orchids thrive in relatively high humidity, mimicking their native tropical environments.

A healthy orchid bloom spike can support many flowers that open in succession over weeks.

Orchids can be propagated by dividing an established plant into separate sections.

Some orchids use mimicry, resembling female insects to trick males into attempting to pollinate them.

Greenhouses allow orchid growers to closely control temperature, humidity, and light year-round.

With proper care, many orchids will rebloom on the same or a new spike each year.

Certain orchid species produce a strong, sweet fragrance to attract specific pollinators.

Title: Peonies
Trivia:
Herbaceous peonies die back to the ground each winter and regrow from the roots in spring.

Peonies grow from thick, fleshy tuberous roots rather than bulbs.

Ants are commonly seen on peony buds, attracted to a sugary secretion, though they don't harm the plant.

Many peony varieties are prized for their strong, sweet fragrance.

Peonies typically bloom for a few weeks in late spring to early summer.

Double-flowered peony varieties have many extra layers of petals compared to simpler single blooms.

Peonies are remarkably long-lived, with some plants thriving in the same spot for decades.

Large, heavy peony blooms often benefit from staking to keep them from flopping over.

The peony is named after Paeon, a healer in Greek mythology.

Established peony plants can be divided to create new plants, though they resent frequent disturbance.

Peony buds start out small and hard before rapidly swelling just before opening.

Tree peonies have a woody, shrub-like structure, unlike the more common herbaceous type.

Peonies have a relatively short bloom time compared to many other perennial flowers.

Peonies are a popular choice for cut flower arrangements, especially in wedding bouquets.

Title: Dahlias
Trivia:
Dahlias grow from tuberous roots that must typically be dug up before winter in cold climates.

Disbudding, removing side buds, encourages a dahlia plant to put more energy into fewer, larger blooms.

Pompon dahlias have small, tightly rounded blooms made of many curled petals.

Dinnerplate dahlias can produce blooms up to a foot across.

Dahlia tubers are frost-tender and can be killed if left in the ground through a hard freeze.

Tall dahlia varieties often need staking to support their heavy blooms.

Dahlias are known for blooming later in the season, often continuing until the first frost.

Thousands of registered dahlia varieties exist, spanning a huge range of sizes and forms.

Dahlias can be propagated from stem cuttings as well as by dividing their tubers.

Gardeners in cold climates typically overwinter dahlia tubers indoors in a cool, dry space.

Dahlia petals can be flat, curled, or quilled depending on the variety.

Dahlias are native to Mexico and were cultivated by the Aztecs long before reaching Europe.

Dahlias are popular show flowers, with competitions judging size, form, and color.

Dahlias are available in nearly every color except true blue.

Title: Hydrangeas
Trivia:
Mophead hydrangeas produce large, rounded clusters of showy blooms.

Lacecap hydrangeas have flat flower clusters with tiny fertile flowers ringed by showier ones.

"Bluing" a hydrangea refers to shifting its bloom color toward blue through soil chemistry.

Aluminum availability in the soil is a key factor in whether certain hydrangeas bloom blue or pink.

Panicle hydrangeas produce cone-shaped flower clusters rather than rounded mophead blooms.

Oakleaf hydrangeas are named for their distinctively lobed, oak-like foliage.

Pruning time for hydrangeas depends heavily on the variety, since some bloom on old wood and others on new.

Hydrangeas are woody shrubs that can range from a few feet to over ten feet tall.

Bloom color in many hydrangea varieties is directly tied to the soil's pH level.

Many hydrangea varieties prefer partial shade, especially in hot climates.

Deadheading spent hydrangea blooms can encourage a tidier appearance, though it doesn't always trigger reblooming.

Climbing hydrangea varieties can attach themselves to walls or trellises using small aerial roots.

More acidic soil tends to produce blue hydrangea blooms, while alkaline soil favors pink.

Bigleaf hydrangeas are among the most commonly grown hydrangea species in home gardens.

Title: Lavender
Trivia:
Lavender's essential oil is widely used in perfumes, soaps, and aromatherapy products.

Lavender is prized for its strong, aromatic fragrance, present in both its flowers and foliage.

Lavender is native to the Mediterranean region, where it thrives in dry, sunny conditions.

Lavender flowers form on tall, narrow spikes above the plant's foliage.

Lavender is highly drought-tolerant once established, making it popular in water-wise gardens.

Dried lavender flowers are commonly used in sachets to freshen drawers and closets.

Lavender is a woody perennial that can live for many years with proper care.

Lavender flowers are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.

Lavender's silvery-green foliage helps it reflect intense sunlight in hot climates.

Regular pruning after bloom helps keep lavender plants compact and prevents them from becoming woody.

The genus name Lavandula is thought to derive from the Latin word for "to wash."

Dried lavender retains much of its fragrance and color for months after harvest.

Culinary lavender is used sparingly to flavor baked goods, teas, and other dishes.

Lavender is a popular choice for low, fragrant garden borders and edging.

Title: Marigolds and Zinnias
Trivia:
Marigolds are often planted alongside vegetables in the belief that their scent helps deter certain pests.

Zinnias are known for their bright, long-lasting blooms in a huge range of colors.

Both marigolds and zinnias are typically grown as annuals, completing their life cycle in one season.

Regularly deadheading marigolds and zinnias encourages the plants to keep producing new blooms.

Marigolds are sometimes used as a natural repellent in companion planting schemes.

Marigolds and zinnias are both considered easy-care flowers well suited to beginning gardeners.

Both flowers are popular choices for bedding displays due to their reliable, colorful blooms.

Zinnias are a favorite for cut flower gardens because of their sturdy stems and vase life.

Marigold and zinnia seeds generally germinate quickly in warm soil.

Both marigolds and zinnias are commonly direct-sown into garden beds rather than started indoors.

Zinnias come in vibrant shades ranging from soft pastels to bold, saturated colors.

Marigolds are a classic companion plant in vegetable gardens.

Both marigolds and zinnias bloom over a long stretch of the growing season.

Marigolds and zinnias generally tolerate heat and short dry spells fairly well once established.

Title: Irises
Trivia:
Bearded irises grow from thick underground rhizomes rather than true bulbs.

Bearded iris varieties are named for the fuzzy "beard" found on their lower petals.

The stylized fleur-de-lis symbol is widely believed to be based on the iris flower.

Irises belong to the plant family Iridaceae, along with crocuses and gladiolus.

An iris flower's lower, drooping petals are called "falls."

An iris flower's upright inner petals are called "standards."

Crowded iris rhizomes benefit from being divided every few years to stay healthy and bloom well.

Some modern iris varieties are bred to rebloom later in the season after their initial spring flush.

Siberian irises tolerate wetter, boggier soil better than many bearded iris varieties.

Some iris species thrive in consistently moist soil, unlike drought-tolerant bearded types.

Iris foliage has a distinctive flat, sword-like shape.

Most iris varieties bloom in mid to late spring.

Irises are available in an extremely wide range of colors, including some near-black varieties.

The iris flower is named after Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow.

Title: Daisies and Asters
Trivia:
Daisies and asters are both members of the large composite, or aster, plant family.

What looks like a single daisy petal is technically one small ray floret.

The center of a daisy or aster flower is made up of many tiny disc florets.

Many aster varieties are perennials, returning reliably year after year.

Asters are prized for extending garden color into fall, when many other flowers have finished blooming.

Shasta daisies are a popular hybrid known for their classic white-and-yellow blooms.

Michaelmas daisies are a traditional name for certain fall-blooming aster varieties.

Both daisies and asters are highly attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.

Deadheading spent daisy and aster blooms can encourage a longer overall flowering period.

Many aster species are native to North America, supporting local pollinator populations.

Daisies are often associated with a simple, cheerful appearance in garden design.

Wild daisies and asters are common sights in meadows and along roadsides.

Both daisies and asters are generally considered hardy, low-maintenance garden plants.

The daisy's simple flower structure has made it a common symbol in art and folklore.

Title: Tomatoes
Trivia:
Determinate tomato varieties grow to a fixed size and ripen most of their fruit around the same time.

Indeterminate tomato varieties keep growing and producing fruit until frost stops them.

Tomato plants grow along a sprawling vine unless supported or pruned.

Heirloom tomato varieties are open-pollinated types passed down for generations, often prized for flavor.

Caging tomato plants helps keep the fruit off the ground and improves air circulation.

Blossom end rot in tomatoes is often linked to inconsistent watering and calcium uptake.

Tomatoes continue to ripen after picking, especially if they're already starting to turn color.

Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family, along with peppers, eggplants, and potatoes.

Suckering removes small side shoots from tomato plants to direct energy into main stems and fruit.

A trellis can support vining tomato plants and keep fruit cleaner and easier to harvest.

Rotating where tomatoes are planted each year helps reduce the buildup of soil-borne diseases.

Tomatoes generally need at least six to eight hours of direct sunlight a day to thrive.

Cherry tomatoes are small, fast-ripening varieties popular for snacking and salads.

Slicing tomatoes are typically larger varieties bred for sandwiches and fresh eating.

Title: Peppers
Trivia:
Capsaicin is the compound responsible for a pepper's heat, concentrated mostly near the seeds and pith.

Bell peppers are a mild pepper variety that starts green and can ripen to red, yellow, or orange.

The Scoville scale measures a pepper's heat based on its capsaicin concentration.

Peppers, like tomatoes, are members of the nightshade plant family.

Pepper seedlings are usually started indoors and transplanted outside after the danger of frost has passed.

A pepper's flavor and sweetness typically increase the longer it's left to ripen on the plant.

Peppers are heat-loving plants that generally struggle in cool or cloudy conditions.

Pepper flowers can self-pollinate, though visiting insects often improve fruit set.

Hundreds of pepper varieties exist, ranging from sweet bell types to extremely hot chilies.

Peppers can be harvested at any stage of ripeness, though flavor changes as they mature.

Spicy pepper varieties are widely used both fresh and dried in cooking around the world.

Sweet pepper varieties are bred specifically to have little to no capsaicin.

Growing peppers in a greenhouse can extend the season in cooler climates.

Tall or heavily fruiting pepper plants sometimes benefit from staking for extra support.

Title: Squash and Pumpkins
Trivia:
Squash and pumpkins both belong to the cucurbit plant family, along with cucumbers and melons.

Many squash varieties grow as sprawling vines that can spread several feet in every direction.

Bush-type squash varieties take up less garden space than traditional vining types.

Squash plants produce separate male and female blossoms on the same plant.

Squash and pumpkin flowers rely heavily on bees and other pollinators to set fruit.

Winter squash varieties are harvested when fully mature and can be stored for months.

Summer squash varieties are harvested young, while their skin is still tender.

A pumpkin's thick rind helps protect it during long-term storage.

Curing winter squash and pumpkins in a warm, dry spot after harvest helps toughen the skin for storage.

Powdery mildew is a common fungal problem that affects squash leaves, especially in humid conditions.

Vining squash and pumpkin plants typically need generous spacing to sprawl without overcrowding.

Pumpkins are usually harvested once their rind has fully hardened and turned the expected color.

Roasted pumpkin seeds are a popular snack made from the seeds scooped out during carving or cooking.

A sturdy trellis can support smaller squash varieties, saving significant ground space.

Title: Root Vegetables
Trivia:
Carrots grow best in loose, well-drained soil free of rocks that can cause roots to fork.

Beets can be grown for both their edible root and their nutritious leafy greens.

Radishes are one of the fastest-growing root vegetables, often ready to harvest in under a month.

Turnips are a cool-season root vegetable often grown in both spring and fall.

Parsnips typically taste sweeter after being exposed to a light frost before harvest.

Many root vegetables grow from a single deep taproot rather than a spreading root system.

Loosening compacted soil before planting helps root vegetables grow straight and unobstructed.

Thinning root vegetable seedlings gives the remaining plants enough room to develop properly.

Many root vegetables can be stored for months in cool, humid conditions after harvest.

Harvest time for most root vegetables is judged by size rather than by color change.

Root vegetables develop their edible part underground, out of direct sunlight.

Most common root vegetables prefer the cooler temperatures of spring and fall over peak summer heat.

Succession planting root vegetables every few weeks can provide a steady harvest over the season.

A layer of mulch can help keep soil temperatures more consistent for developing root vegetables.

Title: Leafy Greens
Trivia:
Lettuce is one of the most commonly grown leafy greens in home vegetable gardens.

Spinach grows best in cool weather and tends to struggle once temperatures rise in summer.

Kale is known for tolerating cold temperatures better than many other leafy greens.

Chard is prized for its colorful stems as well as its edible leaves.

Bolting occurs when a leafy green plant switches to flowering, often making its leaves bitter.

Most leafy greens are considered cool-season crops, thriving in spring and fall.

Cut-and-come-again harvesting lets gardeners take outer leaves while the plant keeps producing more.

Many leafy greens tolerate partial shade better than fruiting vegetables like tomatoes.

Leafy greens are often prized for their high nutrient content relative to their calories.

Baby greens are harvested while still young and tender, often for salad mixes.

Succession planting leafy greens every couple of weeks helps maintain a continuous harvest.

A lightweight row cover can protect leafy greens from pests without blocking light or rain.

Some leafy greens, like kale, are hardy enough to survive light frosts in the garden.

Fresh leafy greens are a staple ingredient in salads and many other dishes.

Title: Berries
Trivia:
Strawberries spread by sending out runners that root and form new plants.

Blueberries require distinctly acidic soil to grow and produce fruit well.

Raspberries are part of the bramble family, which also includes blackberries.

Bramble fruits typically grow on thorny canes rather than low, spreading plants.

Strawberry runners allow a single plant to expand into a larger patch over a season or two.

Blueberry bushes often need soil amended specifically to maintain the acidic conditions they require.

A layer of mulch around berry plants helps retain moisture and suppress weeds.

Netting is commonly used to protect ripening berries from birds.

Most garden berry plants are perennials, producing fruit for many years once established.

Raspberry and blackberry plants grow on woody canes that typically fruit in their second year.

Berry flowers rely on bees and other pollinators to develop into full-sized fruit.

Berries generally don't continue to ripen much further once they're picked.

Regular picking during peak season encourages many berry plants to continue producing.

Excess berries are often turned into jams and preserves to extend their use well beyond harvest.

Title: Melons
Trivia:
Cantaloupes develop a distinctive netted pattern on their rind as they mature.

Watermelons are made up of over 90 percent water by weight.

Melon plants grow along sprawling vines that need significant room to spread.

Melon flowers depend heavily on bee pollination to develop into full-sized fruit.

Judging a melon's ripeness often relies on cues like stem separation, sound, or a sweet smell.

A melon's sweetness develops mainly in the final weeks before it's fully ripe.

Melon vines typically need generous spacing to avoid overcrowding as they spread.

A layer of mulch under developing melons can help keep the fruit clean and reduce rot.

Melons are heat-loving plants that thrive during the warmest stretch of summer.

Harvest timing for melons varies by variety, since some slip easily from the vine when ripe and others don't.

A melon's thick rind protects the sweet flesh inside during growth and handling.

The netted texture on a cantaloupe's rind forms naturally as the fruit grows.

The hollow seed cavity inside a melon contains the seeds surrounded by stringy pulp.

Melons generally need long stretches of direct sunshine to develop good flavor.

Title: Mulching
Trivia:
Mulch is a layer of material spread over soil to help retain moisture and suppress weeds.

A layer of mulch reduces how quickly water evaporates from garden soil.

Mulch acts as a weed barrier, blocking the light that weed seeds need to sprout.

Shredded bark is one of the most common types of mulch used in home landscaping.

Straw mulch is a popular, lightweight choice for vegetable gardens.

Mulch helps insulate plant roots from extreme temperature swings.

Organic mulches gradually decompose, adding nutrients back into the soil over time.

Mulch is typically applied a few inches deep, avoiding direct contact with plant stems.

Organic mulch materials include wood chips, straw, and shredded leaves.

Mulch is a common feature in ornamental landscape beds as well as vegetable gardens.

A generous layer of mulch helps protect the root zone of both trees and smaller plants.

Applying mulch after the soil has warmed in spring helps avoid trapping in excess cold.

Mulch helps moderate soil temperature, keeping roots cooler in summer and warmer in winter.

Since organic mulch breaks down over time, it typically needs to be replenished annually.

Title: Raised Bed Gardening
Trivia:
A raised bed is a garden plot built above the surrounding ground level, often within a frame.

Raised beds generally offer better drainage than gardening directly in dense native soil.

Raised beds are often filled with a custom soil blend suited to the plants being grown.

A wooden or stone frame is commonly used to contain the soil in a raised bed.

Raised beds can improve accessibility for gardeners who have difficulty bending or kneeling.

Raised beds are well suited to intensive planting methods that maximize yield per square foot.

Soil in a raised bed tends to warm up earlier in spring than ground-level garden soil.

The border of a raised bed helps keep soil contained and separate from surrounding pathways.

Raised beds can make weed control easier since fewer weed seeds are present in fresh soil.

Compost is commonly mixed into a raised bed's soil to boost fertility.

Untreated lumber is a popular material for building simple raised bed frames.

Planning a raised bed's layout in advance helps make efficient use of limited garden space.

Because raised beds are elevated, their soil can dry out faster and may need more frequent watering.

Well-managed raised beds can produce a higher yield per square foot than traditional row gardens.

Title: Container Gardening
Trivia:
Potting mix is specially formulated to drain well and support plant roots in a contained space.

A drainage hole at the bottom of a pot helps prevent roots from sitting in standing water.

Container gardening is a popular option for patios where in-ground planting isn't possible.

One advantage of container gardening is that plants can be moved to chase sun or shelter from weather.

A plant becomes rootbound when its roots fill the container and have no more room to spread.

Repotting into a larger container gives a rootbound plant room to keep growing.

Container gardening makes it possible to grow plants on a balcony with no ground access at all.

Glazed ceramic pots retain moisture longer than unglazed terra cotta containers.

Container plants often have different watering needs than the same plant grown in open ground.

Sun exposure can vary significantly across a container's location, affecting which plants will thrive.

Dwarf plant varieties are often bred specifically for success in smaller containers.

A saucer placed under a pot catches excess water draining out the bottom.

Compact plant varieties are especially well suited to container growing.

Container gardening is a versatile option for renters and anyone without traditional garden space.

Title: Vertical Gardening
Trivia:
A trellis gives climbing plants a vertical structure to grow up instead of sprawling across the ground.

Climbing vines like beans and peas naturally reach for vertical supports as they grow.

Wall-mounted planters let gardeners grow plants vertically against a fence or building.

Vertical gardening is especially popular as a space-saving technique in small yards.

An arbor can support climbing plants while also creating a shaded garden feature.

A dedicated vertical structure allows heavier vining plants to be trained upward safely.

A living wall is a vertical surface densely planted with many small plants.

Stacked planting systems let gardeners grow multiple layers of plants in a small footprint.

A sturdy support system is essential for vertical gardening, especially with heavy fruiting vines.

Lattice panels are a common lightweight support structure for climbing plants.

Training a plant's growth direction upward can improve air circulation around its leaves.

An obelisk-style trellis adds a decorative vertical accent while supporting climbing plants.

Vertical gardening techniques are widely used in urban settings with very limited ground space.

Growing plants vertically can improve airflow around foliage, reducing certain fungal problems.

Title: Hydroponics
Trivia:
Hydroponic systems deliver a carefully balanced nutrient solution directly to plant roots.

Hydroponics is a soilless growing method, using water and nutrients instead of traditional soil.

A reservoir holds the nutrient solution that circulates through a hydroponic system.

Aeration of the nutrient solution helps deliver enough oxygen to submerged plant roots.

Inert materials like clay pellets or rockwool are common grow mediums in hydroponic setups.
